cues.text: A Convert from a Poor Family
Andrew Dung-Lac was born Tran An Dung around 1795 into a poor, non-Christian family in Bac Ninh, northern Vietnam.
When his family moved to Hanoi in search of work, the twelve-year-old boy was sheltered and instructed in the faith by a Christian catechist, and was baptized, taking the name Andrew.
A Priest Amid Persecution

Ordained a diocesan priest, Andrew ministered to Vietnamese Catholics during a period when Emperor Minh Mạng had expelled foreign missionaries and ordered Christians to publicly trample on crucifixes to prove their renunciation of the faith.
To evade capture, Andrew changed his surname to Lac and relocated repeatedly to continue his priestly work in secret.
Arrest and Martyrdom
Andrew was finally arrested in November 1839 and, after enduring imprisonment and torture, was beheaded at Hanoi on December 21, 1839.
His death was one of countless martyrdoms during this era of persecution.
The Catholic Encyclopedia's later accounts record victims being burned alive in bamboo cages, dismembered joint by joint, or branded on the face with the words 'false religion.'
A Church Sustained Through Three Centuries

Andrew's feast commemorates him together with 116 named companions — 96 Vietnamese, 11 Spanish Dominicans, and 10 French missionaries of the Paris Foreign Mission Society — who died for the Catholic faith in Vietnam between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries.
The group includes eight bishops, fifty priests, and fifty-nine laypeople, among them a mother of six and a child of only nine years old.
A Nameless Multitude Behind the Named
These 117 canonized martyrs are understood by the Church to represent a far larger, largely unnamed multitude, estimated at anywhere between 100,000 and 300,000 Vietnamese Christians.
They died for their faith across nearly three centuries of intermittent, often savage persecution, one of the longest sustained periods of Christian martyrdom in any single nation's history.
Legacy

Pope John Paul II canonized the group together on June 19, 1988; notably, the communist government of Vietnam permitted no official representation from the country to attend, though some 8,000 Vietnamese Catholics from the global diaspora were present.
Despite centuries of suppression, the Church in Vietnam took deep and lasting root.

By the close of the twentieth century, Catholics constituted roughly ten percent of the Vietnamese population, a growth the Church attributes directly to the enduring witness of martyrs like Andrew Dung-Lac and his companions.
